query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, degradation of the as‐built, fcc Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy is governed by selective oxidation or reduction at grain boundaries that leads to the formation of brittle intergranular phases. This localized alteration of chemistry—particularly involving elements such as Al and Cr—weakens the cohesion of the fcc matrix and promotes stress concentration, which ultimately triggers catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured alloy with a homogeneous, refined fcc microstructure and evenly distributed elemental composition.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to controlled thermal treatments (600–800°C) under two distinct gas environments: an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., ambient air with high oxygen partial pressure) and a reducing atmosphere (e.g., hydrogen-rich environment), while keeping all other parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Temperature of 600–800°C with exposure durations of 100–300 hours; gas compositions precisely controlled to be either oxidizing or reducing; baseline mechanical and microstructural states characterized prior to exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries where selective oxidation or reduction induces the formation of brittle phases (such as alumina or chromia in oxidizing conditions, or dealloyed regions in reducing environments).
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, diffusion of reactive elements (especially Al and Cr) to grain boundaries causes either oxidative formation of brittle intergranular oxides in oxidizing gases or preferential reduction and dealloying in reducing gases. Both cases compromise intergranular cohesion, which can lead to crack initiation and propagation, ultimately resulting in catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous microstructure, samples in oxidizing environments will develop continuous or semi‐continuous brittle oxide scales along grain boundaries accompanied by increased intergranular cracking. In contrast, samples exposed to reducing conditions will exhibit signs of elemental depletion (particularly at grain boundaries), leading to reduced ductility and early mechanical failure.
generation.baseline: As-built alloy with homogeneous composition and microstructure, exhibiting high intergranular cohesion and standard mechanical integrity before exposure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically for exposures within the 600–800°C range and durations up to several hundred hours. Outside of these conditions (for example, significantly lower or higher temperatures or very long exposures), other degradation mechanisms may predominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the selective oxidation or reduction processes and the threshold levels for catastrophic failure remain uncertain, as they may depend on subtle variations in the initial microstructure and local stress states.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a set of controlled thermal exposure experiments at 600–800°C on as-built alloy samples under both oxidizing and reducing gas environments. Use in-situ high-temperature microscopy and post-exposure analysis (SEM, TEM, and EDS) to examine grain boundary integrity, oxide scale formation or elemental depletion, and correlate these observations with mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness, crack density).
measurements: Elemental composition profiles across grain boundaries (via EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microstructural evolution and mechanical degradation in both oxidizing and reducing environments do not significantly differ from the baseline homogeneous state, or if catastrophic failure occurs without the expected intergranular changes (i.e., without formation of brittle phases or dealloyed regions at the grain boundaries), the hypothesis will be falsified.
